messages.subject: Re: Simple question about specifying covariance of error terms for endogenous variables in the model
messages.subject_clean: Simple question about specifying covariance of error terms for endogenous variables in the model
messages.body_plain:
Timothy,
  Your first paraphrase seems correct to me.  The second may be a little too strong, taking us into semantic issues of mapping structural equation models onto substantive theories that have not received sufficient attention in the literature.

  The shared cause with effects of opposite direction is one way to create a negative covariance.  Bayesian causal model literature will tell you that a covariance can always be replaced with a latent common cause but all this means is that one can make this substitution without changing the implied joint probability distribution of the observed variables.  It also reflects the concept of model simplification such that, for example, indirect effects of a common cause through two separate latent mediators, could be simplified by omitting the mediators and modeling the indirect effects as direct effects.

  It does not mean that a common cause offers the a theoretically natural representation of the data generating mechanism.  For example, you could have two common causes, each having opposing effects on the two variables, and perhaps themselves positively correlated.  In this case, a single latent common cause can capture the required variance components, but it does not "cut nature at the joints" by representing the causal variables in terms of attributes that a theorist would find natural.  Instead, one might end up with a complex mathematical abstraction that represents many combined effects of different variables in a mathematically parsimonious but theoretically obtuse way.

  Ultimately, such things take us too far beyond the data and the only way to study them empirically is to develop measures for the hypothesized omitted causes and included them in future studies to test such hypotheses.  A simple covariance or latent common cause offers a parsimonious place holder for mechanisms we did not study and that we may not fully understand.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.body_plain:
Piyush--

1. the two exogenous variables (Function and Condition) are both dichotomous. Therefore I use WLSMV. Is this correct?

No. If you treat Function and Condition as covariates--meaning basically that they are observed variables and predictors only--these dichotomies do not violate the assumptions behind maximum likelihood (ML) estimation. ML only assumes normality conditional on the covariates. I believe that, if you simply omitted your syntax's reference to the covariance of Function and Condition, lavaan's default would be to treat those variables as covariates.

     The provided outputs make reference to a list of 8 "defined parameters," but I do not see these parameters defined in your "Model2" syntax, from your previous message. You name some parameter estimates, but you do not define new parameters. Where do those additional defined parameters come from? They could be implicated in the error message that you are receiving,

     I am also surprised by your "SEM-MI.png" output, which shows the results of the measurement invariance function. This output shows the configural invariance model to have 40 degrees of freedom, consistent with the multiple group models that you show elsewhere.
     The next step, imposing invariant loadings, gains 12 degrees of freedom. I find that surprising, since I see only 6 loadings to be estimated in the model (times 2 groups), and some of those are already fixed to 1. So I cannot myself understand where the gain of 12 degrees of freedom comes from.
     Then, in the following step, which imposes invariant intercepts, degrees of freedom increase by only 5. That is extremely odd--typically, we would expect the gain from constraining loadings and the gain from constraining intercepts to match, unless there is some peculiar specification.

     I believe that I would like to see the syntax that actually produced these results, including the creation of the new "defined parameters."

--Ed Rigdon

messages.subject: Re: Rasch item difficulty parameters: continuous response in lavaan
messages.subject_clean: Rasch item difficulty parameters: continuous response in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
Simon,
  Do you mean the continuous item responses in the unit interval to represent probabilities?  Could you dichotomize the responses at .5 and fit a conventional Rasch model?  Alternatively, could you gently rescale the responses to exclude values of 0 and 1, apply a logit transformation, and then fit a linear CFA to the transformed responses as an approximation to a logistic model?  Could you define the Rasch difficulty and descrimination as defined parameters and then use those to impose equal discrimination across items?  If so, it might be helpful to fit the unconstrained two-parameter model first, just to give yourself a reference point for evaluating the constrained solution.

  Is it safe to assume that you want to estimate parameters for specific items, not the the average across whatever item respondents answered in a particular ordinal position in their test?  If so, you probably need to arrange your data so that the columns represent unique items and the rows represent test takers.  You then have a standard data set up with a missing data issue represented by the blank cells in the data set where a given test taker was not presented with a given item.  That issue is hopefully manageable if you have a very large data set.  Lavaan offers both FIML and MI approaches to missing data.  The models you are fitting assume no order effects, the probability conditional on ability is independent of exposure to prior items.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

Dear Keith,

Thank you very much for your valuable perspectives. If you check the dataset, I have 16004 unique items (item_id) given to 2000 test takers (person_id). But if you look at how these items haven been assigned to the persons, you realize some items have been taken by as many as 347 persons, while some have been taken by only 1 person (overall, the median frequency of using a specific item by test takers is 3 times !red flag! see figure below, there are only 5 unique items taken by >= 200 persons).

So, to make the data wide would mean two things:
(1) I could widen the data such that I have 2000 rows (persons), and `16004` columns for each unique item.
(2) I could widen the data such that I have 2000 rows (persons), and `37` columns for each item_type attempt (e.g., person # 1, took 3 of X type item, 4 of Y type item).

Option 1 for widening the data, would lead, therefore, to the majority of items being barely estimable, right? (because only few people have taken them)
Option 2 for widening the data, would lead, however, to item_type attempts (e.g., each person taking x number of Y type item, w number of Z type item etc.)

If my reasoning regarding the data widening is correct, then it may seem more reasonable to estimate item difficulty parameter really by their type, and not unique items per se, right?

If so, I'm attaching the option 2 widened dataset and would be really interested to know how you would model it and whether you agree with dataset?

Thanks, Simon

messages.body_plain:
Hi Simon,

As I mentioned on CrossValidated (https://chat.stackexchange.com/rooms/107527/discussion-between-jeremy-miles-and-user7148318) SEM is not going to work for this - you have (far!) too many variables, and too much missing data.

A mixed model is equivalent to a single factor CFA - you can fit this in a mixed model - the item intercepts are the difficulty parameters.

The part I don't understand is where you say "The items come with their machine-learned difficulty parameters."

You either estimate them, or you don't. I don't think there's an in-between - unless you want to go Bayesian and use the machine learned difficulties as prior distributions of the parameters. I'd model that using Stan.

Jeremy

On Sun, 3 May 2020 at 10:14, Simon Harmel <sim.h...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Dear Keith,
>
> Thank you very much for your valuable perspectives. If you check the dataset, I have 16004 unique items (item_id) given to 2000 test takers (person_id). But if you look at how these items haven been assigned to the persons, you realize some items have been taken by as many as 347 persons, while some have been taken by only 1 person (overall, the median frequency of using a specific item by test takers is 3 times !red flag! see figure below, there are only 5 unique items taken by >= 200 persons).
>
> So, to make the data wide would mean two things:
> (1) I could widen the data such that I have 2000 rows (persons), and `16004` columns for each unique item.
> (2) I could widen the data such that I have 2000 rows (persons), and `37` columns for each item_type attempt (e.g., person # 1, took 3 of X type item, 4 of Y type item).
>
> Option 1 for widening the data, would lead, therefore, to the majority of items being barely estimable, right? (because only few people have taken them)
> Option 2 for widening the data, would lead, however, to item_type attempts (e.g., each person taking x number of Y type item, w number of Z type item etc.)
>
> If my reasoning regarding the data widening is correct, then it may seem more reasonable to estimate item difficulty parameter really by their type, and not unique items per se, right?
>
> If so, I'm attaching the option 2 widened dataset and would be really interested to know how you would model it and whether you agree with dataset?
>
> Thanks, Simon
>
> #== New widened dataset (by item_type):
> read.csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/izeh/n/master/w2.csv', stringsAsFactors = F)
>
>
>
>
> On Sun, May 3, 2020 at 10:04 AM 'Nickname' via lavaan <lav...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> > Simon,
> >   Do you mean the continuous item responses in the unit interval to represent probabilities?  Could you dichotomize the responses at .5 and fit a conventional Rasch model?  Alternatively, could you gently rescale the responses to exclude values of 0 and 1, apply a logit transformation, and then fit a linear CFA to the transformed responses as an approximation to a logistic model?  Could you define the Rasch difficulty and descrimination as defined parameters and then use those to impose equal discrimination across items?  If so, it might be helpful to fit the unconstrained two-parameter model first, just to give yourself a reference point for evaluating the constrained solution.
> >
> >   Is it safe to assume that you want to estimate parameters for specific items, not the the average across whatever item respondents answered in a particular ordinal position in their test?  If so, you probably need to arrange your data so that the columns represent unique items and the rows represent test takers.  You then have a standard data set up with a missing data issue represented by the blank cells in the data set where a given test taker was not presented with a given item.  That issue is hopefully manageable if you have a very large data set.  Lavaan offers both FIML and MI approaches to missing data.  The models you are fitting assume no order effects, the probability conditional on ability is independent of exposure to prior items.
> >
> > Keith

I think the approach supported by this paper <https://duolingo-papers.s3.amazonaws.com/reports/DRR-20-02.pdf> seems to exactly suite my type of data. It requires a dyadic expansion R function <http://stla.github.io/stlapblog/posts/DyadicExpansion.html> (called num2dyadic) to convert the continuous responses to binary responses.

It seems after this conversion, a 2PL model with known discrimination parameters can be fit. But after the conversion, there is a significant number of 0s but few 1s. So, I'm not sure if I'm doing the conversion correctly.

dat <- read.csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/izeh/n/master/g.csv', stringsAsFactors = F)

dat$item_score2 <- num2dyadic(dat$item_score, nmax = length(dat$item_score)) # the conversion

messages.body_plain:
Simon,
  Option 1 is not an option for the reasons Jeremy gave.  You cannot have more columns than rows in your data set if you want to analyze covariance structures.

  It seems to me that the key issue for Option 2 is whether you expect the variations that distinguish different items of the same type to impact item parameters.  The approach appears to assume that they do not.

  I am have not thought this through, but I wonder if you might want to consider some form of explanatory IRT model.  If, instead of treating every new item as a unique value of a nominal variable with its own parameters, you instead could scale the items in a n-dimensional space of item characteristics, then you could model the item difficulties as functions of those characteristics.  I am wondering whether that might constrain the parameters sufficiently much that even your rare items could be useful and informative.  Just a thought.

Keith
------------------------

messages.subject: Re: Rasch item difficulty parameters: continuous response in lavaan
messages.subject_clean: Rasch item difficulty parameters: continuous response in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
Simon,
  I do not want to speculate too much about the nature of the data or your goals in the analysis because that leads into a garden of forking paths.  This thread is also drifting further away from being a question about using lavaan.

  However, if the Rasch model is appropriate to your data, then you already have a workable measure of item difficulty in the probabilities themselves.  Estimating Rasch difficulty parameters would just translate those into the metric of latent ability.  However, unless I am missing something, the mean probabilities across respondents and the difficulty parameters should rank order the items in the same way.  If the Rasch model is not appropriate and the item characteristic curves cross, then this is not the case.

  It still strikes me that the key assumption in treating items of one type as all the same is that whatever distinguishes different items of the same type does not affect the item parameters.

  When you have multiple items of the same type for the same respondent, then the key assumption would seem to be that the mean probability from multiple items has the same statistical properties as a probability derived from a single item response.  Consider whether the CFA unique variances might be less for a composite than for a single item.  Given the size of your data, it seems reasonable, at least as a first pass, to randomly select one item of each non-missing type for each respondent and analyze the resulting 2000x37 data matrix.  Moreover, there is nothing wrong conducting more than one analysis of the same data, so long as you report the results in a transparent way.  You could at least partially test the above assumptions in ancillary analyses by imposing equality constraints and conducting chi-square difference tests.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/
> >

messages.subject: correlating different set of residuals covariances across groups
messages.subject_clean: correlating different set of residuals covariances across groups
messages.body_plain:
Hi all, greetings from Argentina!

I wonder if anyone can enlighten me here. Let's suppose I have two groups and I ran some configural models and they were nearly ok but, inspecting modification indices, there is room for improvement if I make some adjustments.
For instance, a one-factor model with 10 variables (x1-x10) and two groups (a,b).
When I ran separately CFAs, it looks like x1-x3 residuals of these observable variables have to be correlated in the group a and no adjustments were needed for group b. Furthermore, once I checked x1 and x3´s meanings I found that both items refer to a similar construct in a way that group a (say, Spanish translated items) has an almost identical meaning--so we are good in thinking that there´s a theoretical reason to correlate those.

My question is how to model that (or, likewise, how to model when there are two different set, e.g., group a <- x1 ~~ x2, group b x3 ~~ x4)?? In Mplus I simply used to state different on each model and worked good (i.e., model a = x1 with x2 and model b = x3 with x4) , but can't find a way to do it in lavaan ...and it looks like I read a lot of material and didn' t find this issue. Of course, I'm talking in the context of measurement invariance analyses, I would need to merge both adjustments in a single configural model to start with the other invariance tests.
Thanks a bunch!

Fernan

Instituto de Investigaciones
CONICET
Universidad de Buenos Aires
Argentina

messages.subject: Re: correlating different set of residuals covariances across groups
messages.subject_clean: correlating different set of residuals covariances across groups
messages.body_plain:
You will find that in the lavaan tutorials. When you want to make different specifications for different groups, use the "c(a, b)" modifier. For exam, if you want the residual covariance of x3 and x4 to be free in the first group but fixed to 0 in the second group, you might write:

x3 ~~ c(NA,0)*x4

The "NA" in R says that the estimate is an unknown value for group 1.
If you want the value fixed in the first group but free in the second, just reverse the order:

x3 ~~ c(0,NA)*x4

messages.subject: how to get the correlation-matrix with lavInspect at a manifest path-model
messages.subject_clean: how to get the correlation-matrix with lavInspect at a manifest path-model
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

some years ago I could get the (empirical) correlation-matrix of the variables in my lavaan models with lavInspect(model, "sampstat") after having done the calculations (sem or cfa) using std.ov=TRUE. For some years now this still functions with CFA, but doesn't function anymore with manifest path-models: here, only the endogenous variables are standardized in the correlation/covariance-matrix I get with lavInspect. Because all manifest variables in a CFA are endogenous, I assume that this could be the reason, why I still get the full correlation-matrix at CFA-Models. (It seems to me that the behavior of lavInspect changed at the same time the optimizaion method NLMINB was introduced, but I'm not sure.)
Following the description of std.ov the calculations should be done using the correlation matrix of all observed variables, and there is no hint, that this is restricted to the endogenous variables of the model. So the question seems to be which informations are used by lavInspect.

Now the most important question for me is: Does there still exist a way to get the empirical correlation-matrix at (manifest) path models within lavaan?

Thanks for any answer and of course thanks for this package!

Edgar

messages.body_plain:
On 5/5/20 2:03 PM, Edgar Schoreit wrote:
> Now the most important question for me is: Does there still exist a way
> to get the empirical correlation-matrix at (manifest) path models within
> lavaan?

My guess would be that you have exogenous variables in your model, and
by default, lavaan uses fixed.x = TRUE, implying that lavaan does not
'touch' your exogenous variables.

To get back your full correlation matrix, rerun the model with the
argument fixed.x = FALSE.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
Further to Melissa
the mis-match of scale can cause problems. see
Kim, J.-O., & Mueller, C. W. (1978). Factor analysis: Statistical methods and practical issues (Vol. 14). Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage
Instead of deleting outliers, why not winsorize the scores so that you keep the cases but restrict the range for the extreme scores?
at least you should test the impact of deleting them vs. rescaling them
gavin

messages.subject_clean: Perfect fit but no standard error
messages.body_plain:
If one set of variables falls in the range 1-6 (a Likert-style rating scale) and another variable falls in the range 100 to 1000, the variables have numeric scales of very different range. Not surprising this can cause real problems with calculating variance-covariance matrices. we found this in a 2008 study where we had rating scale values 1-6 and an achievement score M=700, SD=100. We had to reverse transform the test scores to IRT values with M=4.29, SD=1.61. The analysis engine was very happy regressing latent factors onto achievement once we did that.Of course whether logit values or transformed values the test scores had the same meaning, but SEM didn't like it with such a large mis-match of numeric range.

messages.body_plain:
Hello!

I have a 2nd order CFA model: one general factor G and four domain factors v, c, m and s.
I am trying to introduce an observed variable as a predictor, "RW". I want to find out if RW has an effect on any of the domain factors and/ or on G.

1) First I modelled each factor separately and regressed it on RW. (which worked)

2) Second, I modelled G (with a second order model) and regressed only G on RW. (which again, I was able to do)

3) Now, I would like to test if, on top of its effect on G, RW also has an effect on the variance of the some domain factors which is not explained by G

These would be my latent variables
 v =~ x1 + x2 + x3
 c =~ x4 + x5 + x6
 m =~ x7 + x8 + x9
 s =~ x10 + x11 + x12

 G =~ v + c + m + s

# and this is how I tried to model my "question number three":
G + m + s ~ RW

But it seems that all I did was control for the effect of RW on the domain factors BEFORE esitmating G, which is not what I meant. What I wanted to do was estimate G
and THEN regress the residual 1st order factor variances on RW, but I don't know how to specify it, or if it is possible/advisable at all. Can anyone help me out, please?

messages.body_plain:
Federica--
     In most factor-based SEM estimation methods, there is no "before" or "after." Estimation is simultaneous, though there may be many rounds or iterations to obtain final estimates. Typically, that is seen as a virtue because it produces greater statistical efficiency.
     You describe estimating a model where RW predicts v, c, m, s, and then a second model where higher order factor G predicts the same common factors. If RW does predict the four factors, that would explain why a higher order factor works. G is a "latent variable" meaning that it stands for some influence not directly observeable in that model. But once you include RW as a predictor of the four factors, then the variable is no longer "latent," so there is nothing for G to represent.
     In the model where RW predicts indirectly through G, is the path between RW and G strong? That suggests that G is redundant, once RW is present.
     Another way to check this is to look at the model with RW but without G. If there is anything for G to represent, then it would be evident in the residual covariances of v, c, m, s.

v =~ x1 + x2 + x3
 c =~ x4 + x5 + x6
 m =~ x7 + x8 + x9
 s =~ x10 + x11 + x12

v+c+m+s ~ RW

v+c+m ~~ s
v+c ~~ m
v ~~ c

If those covariances are near 0, then there is no room for a higher order factor, once RW is present.

     Of course, we cannot say for certain that G and RW are redundant, even if their correlation is strong. But you may need some other variable in the model that can better distinguish the two.
--ED Rigdon

messages.body_plain:
Federica--
     That additional information is very helpful.  There are a couple of ways to do this. The simplest is to add direct paths from RW to the individual facets along with the higher order G factor. If covariance between G and RW is not too high, then collinearity won't be much of a problem.
     A somewhat more complex approach is to replace the error variances / residual variances for the facets with new common factors, and then let RW predict those. This involves these steps:

1. Create one new factor for each of the four facets and standardize it (to solve the identification problem). You can do that via

v_res + c_res + m_res + s_res =~ 0*x1
v_res ~~ 1 * v_res                                       #one for v, c, m, s

(The operator =~ tells lavaan to create new common factors...it doesn't matter which observed variables appear on the right hand side, as long as the loading is fixed to 0.)

2. Add the relevant "residual" term to the equation for the facet, e.g.:

v ~ v_res

(along with the higher order factor statement C =~ v + c + m + s)

3. Fix the residual variances of v, c, m, s to 0:

v ~~ 0 * v                        # one each for v, c, m, s

You may need to provide a starting value for the path between facet and "residual factor." Take the square root of the residual variance reported in a regular analysis.

4. Add the paths for RW predicting these "residua variances":

v_res + c_res + m_res + s_res ~ RW

Make sure that RW is not predicting the facets v, c, m, s at the same time.

This should work. You probably want to try it adding one facet at a time.

--Ed Rigdon

Hi everyone,

I was hoping someone could shed some light on estimating standard errors for user-defined parameters in lavaan.

I'm trying to estimate a direct and an indirect effect in a simple path model of the form

A -> B -> C
A -> C

There is also an additional set of covariates that affect both B and C (but not A).

I am using the following syntax:

SEM.model <- 'C ~ beta31*A + beta32*B + [covariates...]
B ~ beta21*A + [the same covariates...]
direct := beta31
indirect := beta21*beta32'

SEM.fit <- sem(SEM.model,
               data=dataset,
               estimator="WLSMV")

summary(SEM.fit, nd=5)

My question is:
Is this syntax correct for obtaining standard errors on the parameters 'direct' and 'indirect'? The standard errors I obtain are much smaller for the indirect effect than for the direct effect (factor of ~5). It's possible there is an empirical reason for this, but prima facie it seems odd.

I'd be very grateful for any help you have to offer.

Best wishes,
Jono

messages.subject: Re: Standard errors for defined parameters
messages.subject_clean: Standard errors for defined parameters
messages.body_plain:
Jono--
     You can calculate this for yourself. Way back when, Kenny & Judd (1984), developing a method for estimating interaction models, shared a formula for the variance of the product of two normal variables A and B:

variance (A*B) = variance(A) * variance(B) + covariance(A,B)^2 [squared]

Your parameter estimates are (asymptotically) normally distributed under ML estimation, so you just need the covariance matrix of the parameter estimates, which you can obtain from lavaan--see this very helpful page

http://www.quantpsy.org/interact/acov.htm

--using the vcov() function. If your results are in an object called "fit," then

vcov(fit)

will get you that covariance matrix. Then you could calculate the variance of the product itself. To turn that into a standard error, take the square root and divide by a modifier based on n. You can see from the variances of the original parameters and the reported standard errors how lavaan generates standard errors foe the other parameters. Apply the same modifier to the square root of the variance for the product of parameter estimates, and you should get the standard error that lavaan reports, assuming that you have asked for regular asymptotic standard errors and not bootstrap standard errors.

messages.body_plain:
Jono--
     I'm not sure, but I wanted to make this more concrete and reproducible. Here is some syntax. I hope this example looks something like what you are seeing:

library("MASS", lib.loc="C:/Program Files/R/R-3.6.1/library")
popcov<-matrix(c(1,.3, .5,.3, 1, .3, .5, .3, 1), nrow=3,byrow=T,dimnames=list(c("x","w","y"),c("x","w","y")))
popcov
popmean<-matrix(c(0,0,0),nrow=3)
data<-mvrnorm(n=500,mu=popmean,Sigma=popcov) # I should have used a seed here for max reproducibility
# and maybe smaller n would produce a greater disparity in results
library("lavaan", lib.loc="~/R/win-library/3.6")
mediat.mod<-'y ~ a*w+c*x
              w ~ b*x
              indirect := a*b'
mediat.out<-sem(mediat.mod,data)
summary(mediat.out)
print(inspect(mediat.out,"vcov"),nd=7)
sqrt(.0014310*.0017164)

In this example, the coefficients a and b have covariance 0 to 7 decimal places, so the calculated variance of the product does not include the covariance squared term. I get a calculated standard error for the defined parameter which is a bit larger than the lavaan-reported value (about 0.15 vs 0.13).
     Still, I am also wondering myself whether lavaan's reported standard errors for defined parameter estimates are correct, and how to check that.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Standard errors in this case are calculated by the first-order delta method http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/mediation.html.

For example, the gradient for the indirect effect is (b,a,0). Thus, the corresponding standard error is sqrt(t(c(b,a,0))*vcov*c(b,a,0)).

I have calculated the standard error for the indirect effect using data generated by Edward (but with popmean <- matrix(c(3,-1,0),nrow=3) and n=5000, set.seed=1234).
My standard error =0.01864181, and the standard error returned by lavvan is 0.019 (see code below)

library("MASS")

popcov<-matrix(c(1,.3, .5,.3, 1, .3, .5, .3, 1), nrow=3,byrow=T,dimnames=list(c("x","w","y"),c("x","w","y")))
popcov

popmean <- matrix(c(3,-1,0),nrow=3)

library("lavaan")

# Simulation: sample size = 5000

set.seed(1234)

data<-mvrnorm(n=500,mu=popmean,Sigma=popcov)

mediat.mod<-'y ~ a*w+c*x
              w ~ b*x
              indirect := a*b'

mediat.out<-sem(mediat.mod,data)
summary(mediat.out)
print(inspect(mediat.out,"vcov"),nd=7)

grad = c( 0.416,0.205,0)
vcov = diag(c(0.0015161,0.0020261,0.0017979)); vcov[1,3]=-0.0006302; vcov[3,1]=vcov[1,3]

(my.se.IE <http://my.se.IE> = sqrt(t(grad)%*%vcov%*%grad))

Best regards,
Mariia

> > > > > > Your parameter estimates are (asymptotically) normally distributed under ML estimation, so you just need the covariance matrix of the parameter estimates, which you can obtain from lavaan--see this very helpful page
> > > > > >
> > > > > > http://www.quantpsy.org/interact/acov.htm

> > > > > >
> > > > > > vcov(fit)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > will get you that covariance matrix. Then you could calculate the variance of the product itself. To turn that into a standard error, take the square root and divide by a modifier based on n. You can see from the variances of the original parameters and the reported standard errors how lavaan generates standard errors foe the other parameters. Apply the same modifier to the square root of the variance for the product of parameter estimates, and you should get the standard error that lavaan reports, assuming that you have asked for regular asymptotic standard errors and not bootstrap standard errors.

messages.subject_clean: lavaan ERROR Some between-level (only) variables have non-zero variance at the within-level
messages.body_plain:
Hello, everyone,

i try to do a multilevel analysis (with mediator) with the help of lavaan. I have defined my model as follows:

model <-'

level:1
SRH  ~ 1

level:2
SRH ~ b * sunshine + c * D_lat
sunshine ~ a * D_lat

SRH ~~ SRH
sunshine ~~ sunshine
D_lat ~~ D_lat

SRH ~~ sunshine
SRH ~~ D_lat
D_lat ~~ sunshine

indirect := a*b
direct := c
total := indirect + direct'

If I want to fit:

fit <- sem(model,
           data = sun,
           cluster = "country",
           ordered = c("SRH", "D_lat")
           )

then I get the following "error": Error in lav_data_full(data = data, group = group, cluster = cluster, : lavaan ERROR Some between-level (only) variables have non-zero variance at the within-level. Please double-check your data.

My sunshine variable has more than one expression per country, because different months were surveyed and therefore variance in my level 2 variable sunshine occurs obviously. So all this is supposed to be like this. The question ist how can I communicate this to lavaan? Or am I missing something? With lme4 and brms it was no problem to calculate a multi-level model with my data.

I have spent several hours trying to research it myself and unfortunately have not found anything. I would be very happy if one of you could help me. Thanks al lot!

Dear Mariia,

Thanks so much for your very useful response. I reproduced your delta calculations with my own dataset and the results are very close to lavaan's estimates (although not quite identical). In the current case, they reduce to:

var(a*b) ~ a^2 var(b) + b^2 var(a) + 2a*b*cov(a,b)

That gives me something concrete to work with in understanding the magnitudes of the standard error estimates.

Thank you both for your assistance, much appreciated!

Jono

On 5/7/20 11:36 AM, Piyush Shah wrote:
> I have been trying on my own, have not been able to make it work. Is
> there some problem with making meanstructure = TRUE in WLSMV? So, when I
> run the model for one group (Group A) as
>
>      fit_a <- cfa(model2, data = exp_a, estimator = "WLSMV")
>
> it works. But when I run it as
>      fit_a1 <- cfa(model2, data = exp_a, estimator = "WLSMV",
> meanstructure = TRUE)
>
> I get the same warning message: In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel2,
> lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
> lavaan WARNING:
> The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated parameters (vcov) does
> not appear to be positive definite! The smallest eigenvalue (=
> -4.042715e-16) is smaller than zero. This may be a symptom that the
> model is not identified.

Why are you using WLSMV? If your endogenous variables are continuous,
use ML. Even if your covariates (Function and Condition) are binary.

If you have binary variables, but you treat them as continuous, AND you
ask for the meanstructure, then your model will not be identified, as
the variance of a binary variable is a function of its mean. This
results in a non-positive definite variance/covriance matrix for the
model parameters. Hence the warning.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to run a measEq() test using the marker variable method of model identification. When I try to do this, my model fails. But when I try to run the invariance tests in measEq() using the reference-indicator method, the model can't be identified and I can't estimate standard errors. The loadings look right: the first indicator is indeed estimated to be equal to 1, and the reported degres of freedom are > 0, so the model should be identified.

The model failure seems to be entirely due to the reference variable method as it is applied in the measEq() function, because when I run a multi-group model in CFA without the measEq() syntax the model is identified just fine.

Here is my code:

## Specify unidimensional model

# Model syntax
Unidim <- '
empathy =~ sympathetic + empathic + compassionate + softhearted + tender
'

# Fit the model
UnidimModel <- as.character(measEq.syntax(configural.model = Unidim,
                                     data = data,
                                     ordered = c(
                                       "compassionate",
                                       "sympathetic",
                                       "empathic",
                                       "softhearted",
                                       "tender"),
                                     parameterization = "delta",
                                     ID.fac = "auto.fix.first",
                                     ID.cat = "Wu",
                                     group = "SexCode",
                                     group.equal = "configural"))

# Model fit
UnidimFit <- cfa(as.character(UnidimModel),
                              data = data,
                              group = "SexCode",
                              group.label = c("Male", "Female"),
                              ordered = c(
                                "compassionate",
                                "sympathetic",
                                "empathic",
                                "softhearted",
                                "tender"),
                              test = "Satorra-Bentler")

summary(UnidimFit,
        fit.measures = TRUE)

Warning messages:
1: In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel2, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING:
    Could not compute standard errors! The information matrix could
    not be inverted. This may be a symptom that the model is not
    identified.
2: In lav_test_satorra_bentler(lavobject = NULL, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING: could not invert information matrix needed for robust test statistic

The model still fails when I change other parameters, like switching the parameterization to theta and estimating the model without the satorra-bentler test statistic. The model does run using measEq() if I remove the ordered indicators argument, but that's an important part of the model. I can also estimate standard errors if I change ID.cat to the methods "default" or "LISREL", but I still get an error telling me the following:

Warning message:
In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel2, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING:
    The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated parameters (vcov)
    does not appear to be positive definite! The smallest eigenvalue
    (= 1.027876e-18) is close to zero. This may be a symptom that the
    model is not identified

Thanks!

Best,
Thomas

yourdata[,c("factorvariable1", "factorvariable2")] <-lapply(yourdata[,c("factorvariable1", "factorvariable2")], ordered)

fit <- cfa(Model, data=data,std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE, ordered = c("factorvariable1", "factorvariable2"))

Note that multilevel SEM currently (0.6-5/0.6-6) does not work with ordered/categorical data!

messages.subject: Re: Validity
messages.subject_clean: Validity
messages.body_plain:
Zaied,
It is hard to know exactly what you wish to do based on your question.  One possibility is that you are asking how to evaluate your model with respect to your sample.  You can find two chapters devoted to this in Rex Kline's SEM text.  The basic ethos of R is to create an object and then operate on the object rather than to issue a single command and then obtain reams of output.  So, a typical analysis will involve more than one function.  In lavaan, you might fit a model using a function like lavaan() or sem() and then use additional functions like summary() and lavInspect() to extract further information.  Ultimately, however, model evaluation is something that happens in your head, not in your computer.

A second possibility is you are asking specifically about variance accounted for.  If you use the rsquare=TRUE parameter to the summary function applied ot a lavaan fit object you will see and R-square for each endogenous variable in the resulting output.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.subject_clean: Lavaan simulateData standardized=TRUE
messages.body_plain:
The error sounds like you are providing population parameters that imply correlations > 1 (or variances that exceed 1).  Setting standardized=TRUE does not transform any of your specified covariance-structure parameters.  It merely tells lavaan to automatically choose residual variances that would lead to total variances == 1, so that you don't have to specify them in your population model syntax.  If you know your standardized population values already, you are better off just using those.

messages.body_plain:
> What is the R-Squared value that is produced, as a logistic approach does not really have a direct R squared value?

lavaan uses a probit rather than logit link, but it is essentially the McKelvey & Zavoina pseudo-R-squared value described here: https://stats.idre.ucla.edu/other/mult-pkg/faq/general/faq-what-are-pseudo-r-squareds/

> I ran the equivalent model in PROCESS in SPSS, and got similar results, but different magnitudes of coefficients. Does this difference reflect differences in the approach and algorithms?

If your simultaneous SEM is not saturated, then it contains constraints not reflected in the individual univariate models fitted by PROCESS. Also, it sounds like you might have been using logistic regression, whereas lavaan uses probit regression.  You can read about differences in a textbook such as Agresti's Introduction to Categorical Data Analysis.

The Wu & Estabrook based approach that I implemented is not really compatible with assigning a reference indicator, although I never programmed a check for this circumstance.  The argument ID.fac = "auto.fix.first" assumes that because the first intercept is fixed to zero, the factor mean can be estimated.  However, with ordinal indicators, the intercepts already begin as fixed to zero, so there is no information available to identify your estimated factor means.  An arbitrary single threshold of the marker variable could be fixed to zero to identify the factor mean, but you would have to assign that afterward by adjusting the generated syntax or by using the update() method as shown in an example here:  https://github.com/simsem/semTools/issues/73

Is there a reason you do not want to use the statistically equivalent method of fixing factor means/variances in the configural model (which is the default setting)?

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

Thank you Keith and Terrence for your replies!

Keith: I tested out all of the indicators to see if any of them would make the algorithm work, and none of them did. I'm pretty sure the indicators are ok - I selected them using the AOAA approach described by Adam Meade here <https://meade.wordpress.ncsu.edu/files/2019/03/Guide_to_IRT_Invariance_Tests_in_R.pdf>, and my tests indicated that the items are all invariant. I selected my marker variable, the item "sympathetic", based on the nonsigMaxA criteria described by Woods & Wang (2017).

Terrence: This makes sense to me, thank you for the explanation. Ordinal model estimation is still an adventure for me. The method you described looks great, but I had trouble implementing it in R. However, I also could not get the code that you linked in github to work (issue 73) <https://www.google.com/url?q=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Fsimsem%2FsemTools%2Fissues%2F73&sa=D&sntz=1&usg=AFQjCNGtNt48IiPmVp5y0WBh8diHkABk8w>, even after re-installing the latest dev tools version of semTools. Here is the code I am trying to run to fix an arbitrary threshold of my preferred anchor item:

devtools::install_github("simsem/semTools/semTools")
library("semTools")

## Specify unidimensional model

# Model syntax
Unidim <-
'
empathy =~ sympathetic + empathic + compassionate + softhearted + tender
'

# Fit the model specifying that "sympathetic" serves as the marker variable
UnidimModel <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = Unidim,
                                     data = data,
                                     ordered = c(

                                       "compassionate",
                                       "sympathetic",
                                       "empathic",
                                       "softhearted",
                                       "tender"),
                                     parameterization = "delta",
                                     ID.fac = "auto.fix.first",
                                     ID.cat = "Wu",
                                     group = "SexCode",
                                     group.equal = "configural")

# fix an arbitrary threshold of the specified marker variable to zero
UnidimModelUpdated <- update(UnidimModel,
                              change.syntax = c('sympathetic | 0*t1'))

# Print syntax to see if the syntax changed. I didn't notice any change in my code
cat(mod.metric <- as.character(UnidimModelUpdated))

# Model fit
UnidimFit <- cfa(as.character(UnidimModelUpdated),

                              data = data,
                              group = "SexCode",
                              group.label = c("Male", "Female"),
                              ordered = c(
                                "compassionate",
                                "sympathetic",
                                "empathic",
                                "softhearted",
                                "tender"),
                              test = "Satorra-Bentler")

# Summary
summary(dddUnidimFit,
        fit.measures = TRUE)

As for my selection of the mark variable method: I want to use the marker variable method because I am unsure whether it is reasonable to assume that the latent factor variances are equal for the groups in my data. I can't get evidence for that without estimating more constrained versions of my model. But I can use anchor tests to figure out which items are noninvariant, keeping in mind that anchor tests are prone to false positives. So a data driven identification method seems to be the most principled way to go about making decisions, and the marker variable method appears to offer that. Maybe this bastardized mixture of IRT methods and CFA estimation doesn't make sense - if so, I'd be happy to learn of a better way to do things, though!

Thanks again for your patience and help, all.

Best,
Thomas

> I also could not get the code that you linked in github to work
>

> # fix an arbitrary threshold of the specified marker variable to zero
> UnidimModelUpdated <- update(UnidimModel,
>                               change.syntax = c('sympathetic | 0*t1'))

It is a multiple group model, so make sure to pass the correct number of fixed parameter values (1 per group), e.g., 'sympathetic | c(0,0)*t1'

But the reason it didn't work was a silly bug I just found, where I switched the lhs and rhs of the parameter label (i.e., it was looking to update a parameter 't1 | sympathetic' rather than 'sympathetic | t1').  This is fixed in the latest semTools (0.5-2.925), so your code should work after installing and restarting.

> As for my selection of the mark variable method: I want to use the marker variable method because I am unsure whether it is reasonable to assume that the latent factor variances are equal for the groups in my data.

You don't assume that when you use the fixed-factor approach.  Those are arbitrary identification constraints, which get released once they are no longer needed (i.e., when loadings are constrained to equality).  The estimated variances are not comparable in a configural model just because a reference indicator is used, unless you can somehow verify that the reference indicator is indeed invariant.  But by doing that, you will have gone beyond the configural model anyway, and you can draw your inferences about differences in latent variance from a more restrictive model.

> So a data driven identification method seems to be the most principled way to go about making decisions, and the marker variable method appears to offer that.

Not unless you can verify it is invariant.  Look into Woods (2009) method for empirically selecting an anchor set.  It works pretty well, as long as the majority of items are invariant.  You only have 5 items, so fingers crossed.

https://doi.org/10.1177/0146621607314044 <https://doi.org/10.1177%2F0146621607314044>

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: Unable to estimate measEq() model using marker variable method of identifying common factor variance
messages.subject_clean: Unable to estimate measEq() model using marker variable method of identifying common factor variance
messages.body_plain:
Thomas,
  Roger Millsap characterized measurement invarance as P(item | latent, group) = P(item | latent) which we can re-express as P[group1](item | latent) = P[group2](item | latent).  This latter expression emphasizes the need for referential consistency of 'latent' in both groups.  Or, if it is easier and more concrete, we can index these as latent1 and latent2 and then assert latent1 = latent2 as an assumption of the analysis.  Now suppose that your items all include the word 'quite' in the stem such that respondents in the US consistently interpret this as meaning very much and respondents in the UK consistently interpret this as meaning not very much.  You can use identification constraints to fix the scale of the latent variable in both groups.  You might even find that all the parameters are invariant across groups.  However, you have not actually met the criteria for measurement invariance because latent[US] =/= latent[UK].  You need at least some invariant items to serve as anchor items to assure that latent1 = latent2.  This holds true no matter whether you use IRT or CFA, and no matter whether you use unit variances or unit loadings.  I believe that unit variances in CFA correspond to standard practice of assuming a standard normal ability variable in IRT.  The arbitrary identification constraints merely remove overparameterization in the model to give the variable some determinate scale regardless of what it represents.  The anchor items serve a different purpose, to give the latent variables in different groups a common interpretation, that is, to provide a basis for the assumption that the latent variables represent the same thing in each group.  The choice of anchor items is not arbitrary because non-invariant anchor items would undermine that purpose.  However, anchor items can only do their work if one has already fixed the scales of the latent variables with arbitrary identification constraints.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.subject: Re: Moderated Mediation Model
messages.subject_clean: Moderated Mediation Model
messages.body_plain:
Good timing since I'm wrestling with this at the same time. Like you, I also have multiple DVs, so am running it in lavaan (also I don't like spss).

Hayes does include this in his Process for SPSS (model 74 shown below), but Process doesn't produce conditional indirect effects (he makes special note of this in the book).

A challenge is that you can conceptualize your theoretical model like Preacher, Rucker, and Hayes (first diagram below), or as I'm doing for my model (second diagram). Mathematically, these are the same, but they have big implications for your indirect effects. In the first, the X is moderating the second stage effect in your mediated path. In the first, you've simply got a moderator that also happens to be the mediator. So for my model, I'm only computing unmoderated indirect effects since there's no theoretical reason to expect a moderated indirect effect. And I suspect that the reason that Hayes doesn't include them in Process is because it would be impossible to tell which pathway was which. This may also explain why the Preacher et al model doesn't include a path Through XM (third diagram below).

If you're really keen to calculate your moderated indirect effect, I think you're going to have to use a method involving X+1SD and X-1SD. See, your indirect effect is missing some of what Preacher et al discuss, which would be:
## ind_Y_M_X := a1*(b1+(b2*X))
But of course lavaan can't put a variable into the computed effects. Just for fun, I tried plugging my X variable into the equation and lavaan just laughed at me. But I've seen people calculate this by calculating your x upper and lower limits and creating two equations where the [] are calculated numbers entered by hand.
## ind_Y_M_X := a1*(b1+(b2*[X+1SD]))
## ind_Y_M_X := a1*(b1+(b2*[X-1SD]))
Then you do some tests of significance on the difference, but you may do better reading some dedicated blogs on that.

>
> However, after this, I was confused to find that the scaled fit indices (CFI/TLI) have risen substantially (robust ones did not though) in comparison to what is obtained with the following code:
>
> fit<-sem(model,  data = data,std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE,orthogonal=TRUE, estimator='MLR', missing='fiml')
>

The scaled chi-squared after first (bootstrapped) and second code differed only slightly (YB scaling factor differed in third decimal) and it confuses me that CFI is much more favourable after bootstrap.

Setting estimator = "MLR" sets test="yuan.bentler.mplus", not test="yuan.bentler".   See ?lavOptions description.  The Mplus variant is only asymptotically equivalent to what Yuan & Bentler described.

If the result didn't change much for the hypothesized model, then CFI probably changed because the baseline model's chi-squared changed more substantially.

FYI, setting missing = "fiml" vs. "fiml.x" can yield different behavior too, if you have missing data on exogenous observed variables, "fiml" will still listwise-delete observations with missing data on the exogenous covariates, but "fiml.x" retains them (so the model will be fitted to a larger sample).

messages.subject_clean: Specifying an estimator when invoking Lavaan with a covariance matrix
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I read in the Lavaan tutorial that it is possible to run a model with the covariance matrix. This seems ideal for situations where one cannot share the dataset, but still want to facilitate replication. I am using the MLM estimator as I have complete data that isn't normally distributed. When running this normally, Lavaan reports an additional "Robust" column, with the Satorra-Bentler scaled Test statistic, RMSEA, and other values. I would like to be able to replicate those exact scaled values when running the model with the covariance matrix.

# get the covariance matrix based on my model (model2) and data (r_data), and specifying the estimator - I read that passing here would pass it on to sem().
results.cov <- inspectSampleCov(model=model2, data=r_data, estimator="MLM")

# run Lavaan using the model, covariance matrix. Again, specifying the estimator.
fit.cov <- sem(model=model2, sample.cov = results.cov, sample.nobs=155, estimator="MLM")

However, when running the above, I get an error:
lavaan ERROR: estimator MLM requires full data or user-provided NACOV

If I don't specify the estimator in the call to sem() it works fine, but I don't get the "Robust" column. How can I get the Robust (scaled) values when running sem() with the covariance matrix as input?

thanks

messages.subject: Re: Specifying an estimator when invoking Lavaan with a covariance matrix
messages.subject_clean: Specifying an estimator when invoking Lavaan with a covariance matrix
messages.body_plain:
This cannot be done. ML estimation works with a covariance matrix (or covariance matrix and mean vector) alone because the conditional multi-normality assumption underlying ML means that higher order moments of the data are uninformative--they are exact functions of the lower order moments, so the lower order moments suffice. Robust methods reject the conditional multi-normality assumption and so they require either the data itself or estimates of higher order moments. The lavaan() function includes the WLS.V and NACOV options where you can supply an asymptotic weight matrix providing this higher order information, so you could in principle provide that along with the covariance matrix and someone could use WLS or DWLS estimation and reproduce your results. But that weight matrix is generally very large (and requires large n for stable estimation), and I have not seen a case myself where it was provided.

I have a question concerning good practices when testing invariance in multi-sample structural equation models.

I am currently working with a questionnaire which has been administered to three different groups (three countries, in fact).
This study includes some single-item measures and some latent variables with 3 or 6 items each. I have tested for invariance using confirmatory factor analyses for the latent variables (each construct separately), obtaining partial scalar invariance in all cases. Ok, good.

Now I am proceeding to test the structural equation models to examine my hypotheses pertaining relationships among variables. Do I keep the loadings and intercepts constrained across groups in this last model? (except for those couple of items that are non-invariant, naturally). Or do I start fresh so to say and keep everything free to vary?

Thank you

messages.body_plain:
On 5/18/20 9:18 PM, k stol wrote:
> To be sure: while it could be done for DWLS and WLS using the options
> you mentioned (WLS.V and NACOV), I understand that the NACOV option
> would not be possible for MLM.

It is possible, if you have access to an estimate of the NACOV matrix.
This is (N times) the asymptotic variance matrix of the sample
statistics. If you don't have it, you can't use it. To compute an
estimate of it, you need the full dataset.

This is an example:

library(lavaan)

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
               textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
               speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, estimator = "MLM")
fit

# using sample statistics only
S <- cov(lavInspect(fit, "data"))
NACOV <- lavInspect(fit, "Gamma")

fit2 <- cfa(HS.model, sample.cov = S, sample.nobs = 301, NACOV = NACOV,
estimator = "MLM")

messages.subject_clean: Multi-sample structural equation modeling: good practices for invariance tests
messages.body_plain:
GAT,
  I can tell you what I think would be a good practice but cannot assure you that this is common or accepted practice.

  I would fit the structural model both ways and compare with a chi-square difference test. You can also compare the fit of each structural model to the corresponding CFA (with or without equality constraints).  If the structural model with equality constraints fits as well as the models in which it is nested, then that bodes well.  You can then do the rest of the things that you would ordinarily do to critically evaluate the constrained structural model solution.  If the constrained model does not fit, then at least you have an a priori test of the more general model before you switch from confirmatory to exploratory mode.

  If the structural model is well specified, it should reproduce the same covariance structure among the latent variables that you saw in the CFA.  As a result, you should expect the parameter estimates for the parameters in the measurement part of the full structural model to closely reproduce the estimates that you obtained in the CFA.  If not, that could be a sign if mis-specification in the structural portion of the model.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

> It is possible, if you have access to an estimate of the NACOV matrix.
> This is (N times) the asymptotic variance matrix of the sample
> statistics. If you don't have it, you can't use it. To compute an
> estimate of it, you need the full dataset.
>
> This is an example:
>
> library(lavaan)
>
> HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
>                textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
>                speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '
>
> fit <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939, estimator = "MLM")
> fit
>
> # using sample statistics only
> S <- cov(lavInspect(fit, "data"))
> NACOV <- lavInspect(fit, "Gamma")
>
> fit2 <- cfa(HS.model, sample.cov = S, sample.nobs = 301, NACOV = NACOV,
> estimator = "MLM")
>
> Yves.
>

Many thanks John, good to know I'm not the only one! Your images/diagrams didn't come up (perhaps just email me <https://www.uu.nl/medewerkers/DWWeinberg>?), but I've seen model 74 and so think I've understood that you're saying - X moderating M-Y is mathematically the same as M moderating X-Y, but conceptually different.* My hypothesis regards the latter. My idea was simply: do the mediation (Y_M_X, which we expected, and found) and the moderation (M moderates YX, which we also expected, and found) both still exist when we take them both into account? (Hmm, but maybe I need to give this 'taking both into account' idea more thought - what would it actually mean if one/both of the effects disappeared...?)

And your method for the moderated indirect effect sounds like a good place to go next, I was thinking on much the same lines. I'm glad you were the one to try the "plugging X into the equation" trick - I have had enough of lavaan laughing at me over the past few days ;)

*I think this distinction is what vanderWeele, 2014 <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4220271/> is all about, but not having an epi background, it's taking time to sink in...

On Monday, May 18, 2020 at 3:06:22 PM UTC+2, John Jamison wrote:
> Good timing since I'm wrestling with this at the same time. Like you, I also have multiple DVs, so am running it in lavaan (also I don't like spss).
>
> Hayes does include this in his Process for SPSS (model 74 shown below), but Process doesn't produce conditional indirect effects (he makes special note of this in the book).
>
> A challenge is that you can conceptualize your theoretical model like Preacher, Rucker, and Hayes (first diagram below), or as I'm doing for my model (second diagram). Mathematically, these are the same, but they have big implications for your indirect effects. In the first, the X is moderating the second stage effect in your mediated path. In the first, you've simply got a moderator that also happens to be the mediator. So for my model, I'm only computing unmoderated indirect effects since there's no theoretical reason to expect a moderated indirect effect. And I suspect that the reason that Hayes doesn't include them in Process is because it would be impossible to tell which pathway was which. This may also explain why the Preacher et al model doesn't include a path Through XM (third diagram below).
>
> If you're really keen to calculate your moderated indirect effect, I think you're going to have to use a method involving X+1SD and X-1SD. See, your indirect effect is missing some of what Preacher et al discuss, which would be:
> ## ind_Y_M_X := a1*(b1+(b2*X))
> But of course lavaan can't put a variable into the computed effects. Just for fun, I tried plugging my X variable into the equation and lavaan just laughed at me. But I've seen people calculate this by calculating your x upper and lower limits and creating two equations where the [] are calculated numbers entered by hand.
> ## ind_Y_M_X := a1*(b1+(b2*[X+1SD]))
> ## ind_Y_M_X := a1*(b1+(b2*[X-1SD]))
> Then you do some tests of significance on the difference, but you may do better reading some dedicated blogs on that.
>
>
>
>

Hi all:

I'd like to ask some clarifications concerning how lavaan handles differences among latent means in a multigroup structural equation model comprising three groups.
(I have established full metric and partial scalar invariance and am now comparing means across groups.)

I have opted for the marker item approach, according to which I fix the intercept of the market item to 0.
With 5 latent variables and 3 groups:

x1 + y1 + t1 + w1 + f1 ~ c(0,0,0)*1

Next, I'm estimating the latent intercepts

lat1  ~ c(a1, a2, a3)*1
lat2  ~ c(b1, b2, b3)*1
lat3  ~ c(c1, c2, c3)*1
...
lat5  ~ c(e1, e2, e3)*1

Now, my question is: what are the p-values that the intercept section of the output is producing? In the reference group approach (the default in lavaan, I believe), those refer to the comparison between referent and comparison groups. Do they test the difference between the mean and 0?

I am now testing differences in latent means using:

lat1difab:= a1 - b1

Does this seem valid?

Thank you for your help.

messages.body_plain:
> In the reference group approach (the default in lavaan, I believe), those refer to the comparison between referent and comparison groups. Do they test the difference between the mean and 0?

When group-1's mean is zero, then any other group's mean is by definition the difference from the first group's mean, because x - 0 = x.  So there is no need to use the marker-variable approach.  Differences between groups 2 and 3 are just as easily calculated as (e.g.) a2 - a3, because the reference group's mean cancel's out:

a2 - a1 = a2
a3 - a1 = a3
thus:
(a2 - a1) - (a3 - a1) = a2 - a3 + a1 - a1 = a2 - a3

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Multigroup path analysis issue: Unable to constrain regressions to equality for one out of my four groups
messages.subject_clean: Multigroup path analysis issue: Unable to constrain regressions to equality for one out of my four groups
messages.body_plain:
> the regression parameters for one of my four groups aren't constrained to equality unlike those of the other groups. What could be the issue?

You are only providing one label per parameter, as though it were a single-group model.  To apply the same label across 4 groups (thus, constraining it to equality, so the group.equal= argument is unnecessary), provide a vector of labels (one per group).

Outcome ~ c(b1, b1, b1, b1)*M1

This method provides way more options than the group.equal= argument anyway, like fitting partial constraints, e.g., this constraints the slope to equality for groups 1 and 4, which can differ from groups 2 and 3 (whose slopes are equal):

Outcome ~ c(b1, b2, b2, b1)*M1

> if anyone knows how to make these analyses run faster, please let me know ... I have 300k+ respondents

With an asymptotically large sample, I think you can safely rely on the default delta-method SEs instead of bootstrapping.  Or you could use the Monte Carlo approach, which doesn't require fitting the model 5000 times (only once, then resample parameters instead of subjects, which takes seconds instead of hours).  It is easily implemented in the semTools package.  See the ?monteCarloMed help-page examples for using it with lavaan objects.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
> I am running a 2 factor CFA on a set of questionnaire responses about student teacher relationships. Each teacher completed two questionnaires (one reflecting a positive relationship and another reflection a more strained relationship). So I am hoping to account for the correlation between their two responses by adding the teacher ID as a random effect.

If you only have 2 observations per teacher, I don't think you need MLSEM.  You can simply treat these 2 (sets of) measurements per teacher as repeated measures, and use the methods developed for longitudinal or dyadic data.  Store the data in wide format (positive and strained responses stored as separate variables, not separate rows), and have them each load on separate positive and strained factors.  Then the correlations you are looking for are estimated model parameter (the factor correlation, if you set std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE, as well as the item-specific residual/partial correlations).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
k stol,
  If I may interject, here is what I think that Carl meant.  MTMM matrices are a methodology for evaluating the validity of tests.  Tests require scores that can be interpreted and used.  You could apply the same formula to the first order latent variable correlations and obtain a value.  However, there would be no scores involved in these correlations, they are correlations between latent variables and the whole idea behind latent variables is that they cannot be observed and thus are not scores.  One cannot validate the use or interpretation of scores that are not available for interpretation or use.  What might make more sense is if you were to compute scores for the tests that correspond to each of the first order factors, perhaps by summing the items that load on that factor. Now you have scores that can be validated and you can apply the same analysis to these scores as you would to item scores.  Alternatively, perhaps you mean to use the HTMT value for some other purpose than test validation, in which case you can compute it as described above but need to explain to your readership why you are doing that.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

On Sunday, May 24, 2020 at 9:38:44 PM UTC+1, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > I am running a 2 factor CFA on a set of questionnaire responses about student teacher relationships. Each teacher completed two questionnaires (one reflecting a positive relationship and another reflection a more strained relationship). So I am hoping to account for the correlation between their two responses by adding the teacher ID as a random effect.
>
> If you only have 2 observations per teacher, I don't think you need MLSEM.  You can simply treat these 2 (sets of) measurements per teacher as repeated measures, and use the methods developed for longitudinal or dyadic data.  Store the data in wide format (positive and strained responses stored as separate variables, not separate rows), and have them each load on separate positive and strained factors.  Then the correlations you are looking for are estimated model parameter (the factor correlation, if you set std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE, as well as the item-specific residual/partial correlations).
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
Thank you for responding—worked perfectly (and quickly without the bootstrapping!). I totally forgot about manually coding the constraints in the model (something I've done successfully not too long ago). This might be a follow-up question more appropriate for SEMNET, but I'll ask anyway: How would you go about comparing regression coefficients across groups? This is my first time doing multigroup path analysis with more than 2 groups. When I free a constraint across all 4 groups and my model fit significantly improves, would the next step then be pairwise comparisons—what would that look like?

On Sunday, May 24, 2020 at 6:25:39 AM UTC-4, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> >
> > the regression parameters for one of my four groups aren't constrained to equality unlike those of the other groups. What could be the issue?
>
> You are only providing one label per parameter, as though it were a single-group model.  To apply the same label across 4 groups (thus, constraining it to equality, so the group.equal= argument is unnecessary), provide a vector of labels (one per group).
>
> Outcome ~ c(b1, b1, b1, b1)*M1
>
> This method provides way more options than the group.equal= argument anyway, like fitting partial constraints, e.g., this constraints the slope to equality for groups 1 and 4, which can differ from groups 2 and 3 (whose slopes are equal):
>
> Outcome ~ c(b1, b2, b2, b1)*M1
>
>
> > if anyone knows how to make these analyses run faster, please let me know ... I have 300k+ respondents
>
> With an asymptotically large sample, I think you can safely rely on the default delta-method SEs instead of bootstrapping.  Or you could use the Monte Carlo approach, which doesn't require fitting the model 5000 times (only once, then resample parameters instead of subjects, which takes seconds instead of hours).  It is easily implemented in the semTools package.  See the ?monteCarloMed help-page examples for using it with lavaan objects.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

messages.subject: Standard errors for std.lv estimates
messages.subject_clean: Standard errors for std.lv estimates
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I am running a SEM model using the lavaan package and would like to obtain the estimates for the standardized latent variables (std.lv <http://std.lv>). I would like to get the standard errors for the std.lv <http://std.lv> estimates from the regressions.  I have been unable to get any sensible standard errors for these.

When I run command a) and b) I get standard errors for the unstandardized estimates.

When I run command c) I get standard errors for the std.all estimates.

When I run command d) I get the standard errors, z, p-value, lower confidence interval and upper confidence interval reported as NA.

a)       summary(fit, fit.measures = TRUE)

b)      summary(fit, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)

c)       standardizedSolution(fit)

d)      standardizedSolution(fit, type = "std.lv <http://std.lv>")

I have provided some example code below, using one of the datasets with lavaan.  Please could anyone advise why the standard errors are provided for

the std.all and not the std.lv <http://std.lv>, and if there is a way to get the standard errors for the std.lv <http://std.lv> estimates.

Many thanks

Kirsty

******* Example code *******

library("lavaan")

model <- '

# latent variable definitions

ind60 =~ x1 + x2 + x3

dem60 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4

dem65 =~ y5 + y6 + y7 + y8

# regressions

dem60 ~ ind60

dem65 ~ ind60 + dem60

'

fit <- sem(model, data = PoliticalDemocracy)

summary(fit, fit.measures = TRUE)

summary(fit, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)

standardizedSolution(fit)

standardizedSolution(fit, type = "std.lv <http://std.lv>")

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have a problem that has been puzzling me for the past week.

I am simulating 50 runs of a model and using the output of the lavaan function to estimate factor scores which I was expecting to be something close to N(0,1). Since I am using binary indicators, I use the methods "EBM" and "ML" and I ran a check to see if their estimates were close. To my surprise, the standard deviation from the ML method was something around 2x, 3x times the one observed with "EBM".

Below is the code just before calling lavInspect(). fit measures are good enough,i.e., TLI and CLI close to 1 and rmsea close to 0.

The boxplot for the 50 runs for the 2 methods is as below (also attached). Is there any theoretical explanation for this disparity in sd? Note the difference on the scale of the y axis!

Looking forward to hearing from you,

Hugo

messages.body_plain:
Variances are not model parameters, residual variances are. Residuals variances of exogenous variables are total variances, so the std.lv <http://std.lv> solution coincidentally shows the Habit variance as 1.  The endogenous variables have predictors, so when their total variance == 1, their residual variance == 1 - R^2 < 1.

messages.subject: "Standard Error" of difference of two effect sizes in lavaan
messages.subject_clean: "Standard Error" of difference of two effect sizes in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
Hello All,

In this answer <https://stats.stackexchange.com/a/258583/140365>, Dr. Cheung demonstrates how to calculate the "Standard Error" of a pre-post effect size using lavaan.

Suppose, however, we have two independent pre-post effect sizes: one from a "Control", another from a "Treatment" group. Then, we subtract and scale them like so:

New.Effect.Size = (M.dif.gr.T/Sd.dif.gr.T) − (M.dif.gr.C /Sd.dif.gr.C) / ((Sd.dif.gr.C  + Sd.dif.gr.T)/2)

where M.dif is the difference between the means of pre- and post-tests of each group. And Sd.dif is the standard deviation of the difference scores for each of the two independent groups.

I was wondering given this answer <https://stats.stackexchange.com/a/258583/140365> by Dr. Cheung, how I can calculate the "Standard Error" of my "New.Effect.Size"?

Thank you for your time and consideration, Reza

#== Some input values
n.gr.C = 25
n.gr.T = 35
m.dif.gr.C = 25
m.dif.gr.T = 31
sd.dif.gr.C = 1.1
sd.dif.gr.T = 1.7

--

Dear Dr. Jorgensen,

Thank you for your insightful comments. To be clear, I want to obtain the "Standard Error" for: SMD.dif.T -  SMD.dif.C / ( [sqrt(sd_pre.C^2+sd_post.C^2-2*sd_pre.C*sd_post.C*r) + sqrt(sd_pre.T^2+sd_post.T^2-2*sd_pre.T*sd_post.T*r)] / 2 ) as defined in my 2 effect size models below.

Would you please assist me in demonstrating this?

Many thanks, Reza

#--------- Effect size for Control group (everything ends in ".C"):
library("lavaan")
## Sample correlation matrix between pre- and post-test scores
lower.C <- '1
           .5 1'
( Cov.C <- getCov(lower, diag = TRUE, names = c("x_pre.C","x_post.C")) )

## Sample means for the pre- and post-test scores
Mean.C <- c(10, 13)

## Sample size
N.C <- 50

model.C <- '# Label the sds with sd_pre and sd_post
eta_pre.C = ~ sd_pre.C*x_pre.C
eta_post.C = ~ sd_post.C*x_post.C

# r: correlation betwen pre- and post-test
eta_pre.C ~ r*eta_post.C

# Fix the error variances at 0
x_pre.C ~ 0*x_pre.C
x_post.C ~ 0*x_post.C

# Label the means with m_pre and m_post
x_pre.C ~ m_pre.C*1
x_post.C ~ m_post.C*1

# Calculate the effect sizes using sd of difference score as the standardizer:
SMD.dif.C := (m_post.C - m_pre.C) / sqrt(sd_pre.C^2+sd_post.C^2-2*sd_pre.C*sd_post.C*r) '

fit.C <- cfa(model.C, sample.cov = Cov.C, sample.mean = Mean.C,
            sample.nobs= N.C, std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE,
            sample.cov.rescale = FALSE)

#--------- Effect size for Treatment group (everything ends in ".T"):
lower.T <- '1
           .6 1'
( Cov.T <- getCov(lower, diag = TRUE, names = c("x_pre.T","x_post.T")) )

## Sample means for the pre- and post-test scores
Mean.T <- c(12, 16)

## Sample size
N.T <- 39

model.T <- '# Label the sds with sd_pre and sd_post
eta_pre.T = ~ sd_pre.T*x_pre.T
eta_post.T = ~ sd_post.T*x_post.T

# r: correlation betwen pre- and post-test
eta_pre.T ~ r*eta_post.T

# Fix the error variances at 0
x_pre.T ~ 0*x_pre.T
x_post.T ~ 0*x_post.T

# Label the means with m_pre and m_post
x_pre.T ~ m_pre.T*1
x_post.T ~ m_post.T*1

# Calculate the effect sizes using sd of difference score as the standardizer:
SMD.dif.T := (m_post.T - m_pre.T) / sqrt(sd_pre.T^2+sd_post.T^2 -2*sd_pre.T*sd_post.T*r) '

fit.T <- cfa(model.T, sample.cov = Cov.T, sample.mean = Mean.T,
             sample.nobs= N.T, std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE,
             sample.cov.rescale = FALSE)

messages.subject: Re: "Standard Error" of difference of two effect sizes in lavaan
messages.subject_clean: "Standard Error" of difference of two effect sizes in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
Dr. Jorgensen,

I found a typo in my previous model syntax. Here is the corrected version. My apologies. -- Reza

#--------- Effect size for Control group (everything ends in ".C"):

library("lavaan")
## Sample correlation matrix between pre- and post-test scores
lower.C <- '1
           .5 1'
( Cov.C <- getCov(lower, diag = TRUE, names = c("x_pre.C","x_post.C")) )

## Sample means for the pre- and post-test scores
Mean.C <- c(10, 13)

## Sample size
N.C <- 50

model.C <- '# Label the sds with sd_pre and sd_post
eta_pre.C = ~ sd_pre.C*x_pre.C
eta_post.C = ~ sd_post.C*x_post.C

# r: correlation betwen pre- and post-test

eta_pre.C ~~ r*eta_post.C

# Fix the error variances at 0

x_pre.C ~~ 0*x_pre.C
x_post.C ~~ 0*x_post.C

# Label the means with m_pre and m_post
x_pre.C ~ m_pre.C*1
x_post.C ~ m_post.C*1

# Calculate the effect sizes using sd of difference score as the standardizer:
SMD.dif.C := (m_post.C - m_pre.C) / sqrt(sd_pre.C^2+sd_post.C^2-2*sd_pre.C*sd_post.C*r) '

fit.C <- cfa(model.C, sample.cov = Cov.C, sample.mean = Mean.C,
            sample.nobs= N.C, std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE,
            sample.cov.rescale = FALSE)

#--------- Effect size for Treatment group (everything ends in ".T"):

lower.T <- '1
           .6 1'
( Cov.T <- getCov(lower, diag = TRUE, names = c("x_pre.T","x_post.T")) )

## Sample means for the pre- and post-test scores
Mean.T <- c(12, 16)

## Sample size
N.T <- 39

model.T <- '# Label the sds with sd_pre and sd_post
eta_pre.T = ~ sd_pre.T*x_pre.T
eta_post.T = ~ sd_post.T*x_post.T

# r: correlation betwen pre- and post-test

eta_pre.T ~~ r*eta_post.T

# Fix the error variances at 0

x_pre.T ~~ 0*x_pre.T
x_post.T ~~ 0*x_post.T

# Label the means with m_pre and m_post
x_pre.T ~ m_pre.T*1
x_post.T ~ m_post.T*1

# Calculate the effect sizes using sd of difference score as the standardizer:
SMD.dif.T := (m_post.T - m_pre.T) / sqrt(sd_pre.T^2+sd_post.T^2 -2*sd_pre.T*sd_post.T*r) '

fit.T <- cfa(model.T, sample.cov = Cov.T, sample.mean = Mean.T,
             sample.nobs= N.T, std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE,
             sample.cov.rescale = FALSE)

On 5/29/20 11:09 PM, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
>     Do you have any insight into these warnings?
>
>       1: In if (attr(x, "information") == "observed") { :
>        the condition has length > 1 and only the first element will be used

This will be due to a change in lavaan 0.6-6: the information= (and
related options) can (optionally) be a vector of 2 elements, eg
information = c("observed", "expected"). The first one is used to
compute vcov (and hence the standard errors). The second one is only
used for the test statistic. Decoupling this turns out to be useful in
some settings.

>     2: In cbind(c1, c2, deparse.level = 0) :
>        number of rows of result is not a multiple of vector length (arg 1)

> I think this follows from the first warning

Indeed.

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
> Below you can find my syntax and the output. I would be very grateful
> for any help or ideas.

A few things you could try:

1) provide better starting values for those parameters that are now
completely 'off' Eg.,

y ~~ start(10)*y

will use '10' as the starting value the (residual) variance of y

2) temporarily fix more parameters (to reasonable values) until it
converges; then release them one by one, to find out which one(s) are
the problematic one

3) try to put lower bounds on the variance terms, eg

y ~~ lower(0.001)*y

puts a lower bound of 0.001 for this variance.

4) try the experimental option bounds = TRUE and let me know if it
worked or not.

Yves.
